editorial.headline: Processed Fish Retail: Nationally Open, Blocked for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This retail activity spans salted, dried and other processed seafood products, but foreign-investment registration in Bali is blocked by the province-wide moratorium.
editorial.body:
This activity is the retail sale of processed fish, shrimp and shellfish products. Its scope includes salted or dried seafood, alongside products such as fish sausage, fish balls and shredded fish. The examples range across anchovy, shark, scad, grouper and other fish, as well as shrimp, tiny shrimp, squid, clams, mussels and shellfish. The classification is deliberately broad in its retail setting: it covers sales conducted inside a building as well as relevant trade from roadside stalls, shop-front verandas, and movable or pushable market stalls.

That breadth matters because the activity describes the point of sale, not a single product format or a single retail environment. A business may register it for the retail trade of varied processed seafood products, whether the offering is anchored in dried and salted goods or in processed forms such as sausage, fish balls and shredded fish. It is open across the full listed scale range: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. The record therefore gives the activity room to serve small retail operations and larger businesses within the same classification.

Nationally, the PMA position is open. Foreign ownership is permitted up to 100%, under the cited Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021 basis. In national terms, that is a clear position: foreign investment may enter this retail activity, and the listed business scales are all open to it. There is no lower foreign-ownership cap in the record to qualify that national ceiling.

Bali is the decisive exception. A foreign-investment company cannot register this activity in Bali today. At the Besar scale, every scope is assessed in OSS as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah risk, placing the activity within Bali’s moratorium. The provincial rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA, island-wide and permanently; this record identifies the moratorium as taking effect in May 2026. The national 100% ceiling remains the national position, but it does not overcome Bali’s registration block.
